I've been working this land for 35 years. I know what grows here, what the soil wants, and what my neighbors do — and mostly we all do the same things because they work. I'm one person managing 20 mu alone, so I can't afford to experiment or take risks. I need reliable yields I can count on.

My plan is simple: keep the wheat-maize rotation on 12 mu — that's my stable income. Use the remaining 8 mu for cotton, which pays better per mu but takes more work and spraying. I won't change this. It's what I've always done.

For wheat, I'll plant an improved local variety — I buy seeds from the township supply station each year, same as always. I'll rotary till after maize harvest, then sow in mid-October. Three irrigations: once at planting, once at jointing, once at heading. Fertilizer goes down at sowing (compound) and I top-dress urea at jointing. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide in winter, one for aphids and rust in spring.

For maize, I direct seed right after wheat harvest in June. No-till saves me time and the soil stays moist. Hybrid seed — the sales rep at the village store recommends the same one every year. Two irrigations if it's dry. I side-dress urea at the V6 stage. Two sprays for stem borer and fall armyworm if needed.

For cotton, I start seedlings in April and transplant in early May. This crop takes the most work — I spray 8 times across the season for bollworm, aphids, and whitefly. Five irrigations. I apply base fertilizer before planting, then top-dress twice during boll development.
